title: Stop Watching the Scoreboard
author: Whitney Whealdon
summary: Whitney Whealdon opens the first post of a three-part series with Nick Saban's "process" philosophy, in which players stop staring at the scoreboard and focus on executing each play well. She connects it to lead and lag measures from The Four Disciplines of Execution, arguing that the outcome we want cannot be directly controlled and that fixating on it can get in the way. Applied to reading, the scoreboard is the end-of-year test score, and the real vision is students who are better readers, thinkers, and communicators. She warns that treating assessments as both the measure of success and the blueprint for improvement narrows instruction to the discrete skills a test happens to sample. Her proposed alternative is to agree on a vision, redesign instruction and assessment systems around it, support implementation with tools like Louisiana's ELA Guidebooks, and look at patterns across data over time rather than single points.
points: Measuring performance is not the same as improving it, so a test result tells leaders how students did on particular texts but not what instruction will build general comprehension.
Teaching to the assessed skills replaces a rich vision of reading with the narrow goal of answering certain question types correctly.
The sequence she recommends is vision first, then process design, then evidence used to judge progress, with the curriculum as the main tool that models the vision for teachers.
Implementation needs explicit modeling for teachers and tiered supports tied to the shared vision rather than a generic MTSS framework.
Leaders should read trends across assessments and observations over time instead of reacting to a single data point.
quotes: In both philosophies, the end outcome is still desirable, but both acknowledge that trying to directly control the outcome often gets in the way of achieving it.

While we cannot directly produce a test score or guarantee an outcome, we can design and improve the experiences and create the conditions that increase the likelihood of achieving a desired learning vision.
In education, we too often worry about the scoreboard and lose sight of the learning process needed to develop better readers, thinkers, and communicators.

Similarly, students might answer comprehension questions correctly without developing a robust understanding of the text. Performance on a measure is only one piece of evidence that we’re making progress toward our vision.
Yet we typically treat assessments as both the measure of success and the blueprint for achieving it.
We start with the vision, design the process to realize it, and use evidence to help us judge whether we’re making progress.
The biggest and most helpful tool we can provide to teachers is a high-quality curriculum that models what it takes instructionally to achieve the vision.
Assessments help us evaluate our progress, but they shouldn’t define what we’re trying to accomplish.
